title_ar: مصير الروح عندما يقبضها ملك الموت
title_en: The Fate of the Soul When the Angel of Death Takes It
body_ar:
هل تعاد الروح إلى الميت حتى يرد على الملائكة فقط، أم أنها تبقى معه؟

أن الروح عندما يقبضها ملك الموت لا تبقى في يده طرفة عين، وإنما يسلمها إلى ملائكة قدر مد البصر مادي أيديهم أخرجوا أنفسكم، فيسلم هذه الروح إلى هؤلاء الملائكة، فإن كانت الروح طيبة جعلوها في كفن من أكفان الجنة، وطيبوها من طيب الجنة فارتفعوا بها، فإذا استأذنوا عند أبواب السماء قيل: مرحبا بالنفس الطيبة، فأذن لها حتى تخر ساجدة تحت العرش ثم يقال لها: ارجعي من حيث أتيت فيؤذن لها فترجع إلى البدن حتى يسأل الشخص سؤال الملكين،

وإن كانت الروح خبيثة جعلها أولئك الملائكة في سفط من أسفاط النار، ولطخوها بنتن جهنم، ثم حملوها فإذا استأذنوا في أبواب السماء لم يؤذن لهم، {لا تفتح لهم أبواب السماء ولا يدخلون الجنة حتى يلج الجمل في سم الخياط وكذلك نجزي المجرمين} فإذا وصلوا إلى ذلك المكان لم يؤذن لهم وأمروا أن يرجعوا بالنفس الخبيثة من حيث أتت فترد حتى يتم السؤال، وعلى هذا فإن النفس ستبقى في فناء القبر، وقد ورد في أنفس الشهداء أنها تكون في حواصل طير خضر تتفيأ في أرواح الجنة، ولكن هذا بالإمكان أن يكون تمثيلا لهذه الأرواح وأن تكون هي في أفنية القبور، والله أعلم بحقيقة ذلك فلا يبحث عن الكيفيات فيه وإنما يعلم بالضرورة أنها سترجع ويعلم أنها لا تفنى حتى يبعث الجسم وحتى تركب عظامه كما كانت، {أيحسب الإنسان أن لن نجمع عظامه بلى قادرين على أن نسوي بنانه} بالنسبة لسؤال الملكين الذي يبدو أنه لكل الأمم ولا يختص بهذه الأمة وحدها، فهو نظير عذاب القبر، وقد كان اليهود يعرفون عذاب القبر ولذلك ثبت عن عائشة رضي الله عنها في الصحيح أن امرأة من اليهود جلست عندها فاستعاذت من عذاب القبر فأنكرت عليها عائشة ذلك، فقالت: أيعذب صاحب القبر فقالت: نعم، فسألت رسول الله (ص) فصدقها، وكان رسول الله (ص) يأمر الناس بالاستعاذة من عذاب القبر، وكان ذات ليلة مع أصحابه فسمعوا أصواتا مروعة فقال: تلك أصوات اليهود تعذب في قبورها، فعذاب القبر نظير سؤال الملكين فإذا كانت الأمم السابقة تعذب في قبورها فكذلك تسأل، ولم يرد في هذا نص صريح في السؤال أعلمه لكن إذا سئل الناس في الأمم السابقة فإنما يسألون عن أنبيائهم، لا يسألون عن محمد (ص) وإنما يسأل عنه أهل هذه الأمة.
body_en:
Is the soul returned to the dead person only so that he may answer the angels, or does it remain with him?

When the angel of death takes the soul, it does not remain in his hand for the blink of an eye. Rather he hands it over to angels stretching as far as the eye can see, extending their hands: 'Give up your souls!' So he hands this soul over to those angels. If the soul is a good one, they place it in a shroud from the shrouds of the Garden and perfume it with the perfume of the Garden, and they ascend with it. When they ask permission at the gates of heaven it is said: 'Welcome to the good soul,' and permission is given for it, until it falls down prostrate beneath the Throne. Then it is said to it: 'Return from where you came.' Permission is given for it and it returns to the body, so that the person may be put to the questioning of the two angels.

And if the soul is a foul one, those angels place it in a basket from the baskets of the Fire and smear it with the stench of Hell, and then they carry it. When they seek permission at the gates of heaven, permission is not given them: {The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter the Garden until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. Thus do We recompense the criminals} (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:40). When they reach that place permission is not given them, and they are commanded to return with the foul soul to where it came from. So it is sent back, until the questioning is completed. On this account the soul will remain in the precinct of the grave. It has come down concerning the souls of the martyrs that they are in the crops of green birds that take shade among the breezes of the Garden — but it is possible that this is a likeness drawn for these souls, and that they are in the precincts of the graves. God knows best the reality of that, so the modalities of it are not to be inquired into. What is known of necessity is only that it will return, and that it does not pass away until the body is raised and its bones are put together as they were: {Does man suppose that We shall not gather his bones? Indeed, We are able to set right his very fingertips} (Sūrat al-Qiyāmah 75:3–4).

As for the questioning of the two angels — which appears to be for all the communities and not peculiar to this community alone — it is the counterpart of the punishment of the grave. The Jews used to know of the punishment of the grave. That is why it is established from ʿA'isha, God be pleased with her, in the Sahih, that a Jewish woman sat with her and sought refuge from the punishment of the grave, and ʿA'isha rejected that from her. She said: 'Is the occupant of the grave punished?' She said: 'Yes.' So she asked the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and he confirmed her. The Messenger of God used to command people to seek refuge from the punishment of the grave. And one night he was with his Companions and they heard terrifying sounds, and he said: 'Those are the voices of the Jews, being punished in their graves.' So the punishment of the grave is the counterpart of the questioning of the two angels; and if the earlier communities are punished in their graves, then they are questioned likewise. No explicit text on the questioning has come down in this matter that I know of; but if the people of the earlier communities are questioned, they are questioned only about their own prophets. They are not asked about Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him; only the people of this community are asked about him.

flags.arabic: تلك أصوات اليهود تعذب في قبورها
flags.context: the report the Sheikh quotes about sounds heard at night
options: render literally, as the report the Sheikh quotes
render with an editorial frame identifying it as a prophetic report
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW. The record names Jews twice: once in a report of the Prophet identifying voices heard from graves, and once in the narrative about ʿA'isha and a Jewish woman, where the Jewish woman is in fact the one who is right and is confirmed by the Prophet. Translated faithfully, neither softened nor strengthened. The Sheikh gives no narrator, collection or grading for the first report and none has been supplied; for the ʿA'isha narrative he says it is established 'in the Sahih' and that attribution has been kept exactly as he gives it, without specifying which Sahih, because he does not.

flags.context: the report about the souls of the martyrs
options: take shade among the breezes of the Garden (reading arwāḥ as 'breezes')
take shade among the shades of the Garden (reading ظلال, as the parallel passage in record 565 has it)
move about among the spirits of the Garden
flags.note: The verb tatafayyaʾ means to seek shade, which fits ẓilāl ('shades') far better than arwāḥ, and the parallel passage in record 565 of this same slice does read ظلال الجنة. This may therefore be a transcription corruption. The source reading is preserved in body_ar and not corrected; the English takes arwāḥ in its sense of 'breezes', which is at least idiomatic with the verb. Flagged for a reviewer to resolve against the underlying report.

flags.arabic: ولم يرد في هذا نص صريح في السؤال أعلمه
flags.context: the Sheikh's own qualification at the end of the answer
options: render the qualification in full, as a limit on his own knowledge
render as a flat statement that no text exists
omit as a formula of modesty
flags.note: This is the point in the record where the Sheikh explicitly stops short. He says that no explicit text on the questioning of earlier communities has come down 'that I know of', and the whole preceding inference rests on an analogy with the punishment of the grave which he introduces with yabdū, 'it appears'. Neither hedge may be dropped, and the English must not present the conclusion as settled. He leaves the question open and the English leaves it open.

flags.arabic: سفط من أسفاط النار … فناء القبر / أفنية القبور
flags.context: two concrete images in the answer
options: a basket from the baskets of the Fire; the precinct of the grave
a casket from the caskets of the Fire; the courtyard of the grave
a container; the area around the grave
flags.note: safaṭ is a woven basket or casket, set deliberately against the 'shroud from the shrouds of the Garden' in the parallel clause. fināʾ is the open forecourt of a dwelling, and the Sheikh is using it as a technical location for the soul between death and the resurrection; 'precinct' keeps the architectural figure that 'area around' loses.

translator_notes: The date carried here is the CMS record date. Across this whole slice the site serves a bulk-upload timestamp of 19-21 December 2010, which is when the written archive was loaded into the site, not when the Sheikh gave the answer. date_is_cms_upload is set true. The real date of composition is not recoverable from the page and has not been guessed.
Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The source writes the eulogy after the Prophet's name sometimes in full and sometimes as the abbreviation (ص). Both are rendered as 'peace and blessings be upon him'; the source form is preserved in body_ar.

The phrase مادي أيديهم أخرجوا أنفسكم echoes the wording of Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:93 without being marked as a quotation in the source; it has been rendered as part of the Sheikh's own sentence, as he gives it, and not set in Qur'anic braces.
The two Qur'anic quotations are given in the source without references; the references have been supplied per house style.
The Sheikh raises the possibility that the report about the green birds is a figure (tamthīl) rather than a literal description. He does not decide it, and the English does not decide it either.
